section_summary: These pages document U.S. efforts to stabilize Japan’s economy through budget balance, tax collection, credit and price controls, increased exports, and a single exchange rate. They also record debate over aid to Asia, Japan’s prospects for self-support, the authority of the Far Eastern Commission, and post-treaty assistance. The final pages turn to trade reporting and a new free enterprise policy for the Ryukyu Islands; the proclamation continues beyond page 60.

subfiles.title: Soviet press prints Panyushkin speech on Japan
subfiles.about: Reports publication of a Soviet speech on Japan’s economic development.
subfiles.summary: Soviet press printed Panyushkin’s December 2 Far Eastern Commission speech.

subfiles.title: Authorization to present U.S. economic stabilization views
subfiles.about: Authorizes immediate presentation of the attached U.S. position.
subfiles.summary: Authorizes the U.S. member to inform the Commission of the government’s stabilization views.

subfiles.title: Economic Stabilization in Japan
subfiles.about: Sets out U.S. objectives for an immediate Japanese stabilization program.
subfiles.summary: Calls for budget balance, tax enforcement, credit limits, wage and price stability, stronger trade controls, production and food collection. It anticipates a single exchange rate within three months.

subfiles.title: National Security Council action on economic stabilization
subfiles.about: Forwards the Council’s concurrence in a directive to MacArthur.
subfiles.summary: The Council concurred in the Army’s stabilization directive as consistent with NSC 13/2.

subfiles.title: Army letter on MacArthur messages and proposed Japan visit
subfiles.about: Seeks State Department support and participation in a Japan visit.
subfiles.summary: Draper encloses messages with MacArthur and urges a visit with Royall and Dodge, or Nitze’s participation.

subfiles.title: Appeal to Joseph M. Dodge
subfiles.about: Urges Dodge to accept responsibility for Japan’s economic stabilization.
subfiles.summary: Lovett stresses Dodge’s experience and promises State Department support.

subfiles.title: Army request for views on SCAP’s self-support assumptions
subfiles.about: Requests assessment of assumptions behind SCAP’s economic rehabilitation program.
subfiles.summary: Draper asks whether expanded U.S. aid to Asia and favorable regional conditions can support SCAP’s projection of Japanese self-support by 1953.

subfiles.title: Recommendation to answer Draper
subfiles.about: Recommends signing a reply on SCAP’s assumptions.
subfiles.summary: Identifies the two assumptions at issue and recommends the attached reply.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs clearance comment
subfiles.about: Comments on the draft reply to Draper.
subfiles.summary: FE says the reply should address whether the assumptions are prerequisites for Japanese self-support.

subfiles.title: Revised recommendation to answer Draper
subfiles.about: Renews the recommendation to sign a reply on SCAP’s assumptions.
subfiles.summary: Restates the assumptions and recommends signing the attached letter.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on SCAP’s economic assumptions
subfiles.about: Qualifies the assumptions supporting SCAP’s long-term projections.
subfiles.summary: Lovett says no integrated Asian aid program has been adopted and future trade conditions cannot be predicted. He supports describing the 1950 appropriation as progress toward self-support, without committing to SCAP’s 1951–53 projections.

subfiles.title: Comments on Economic Implementation of U.S. Far East Policy
subfiles.about: Criticizes proposed trade orientation and assumptions about Soviet control.
subfiles.summary: Brown questions diverting Japanese trade from North China and Manchuria and warns against language suggesting an Asian ERP.

subfiles.title: Economic Implementation of U.S. Policy with Respect to the Far East
subfiles.about: Critiques a proposed coordinated U.S. economic aid program for Asia.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum disputes assumptions that China will be Soviet-controlled and that selected Asian countries form a coherent economic group. It argues that an ERP-style program would be costly and difficult to administer, while U.S. commercial policy offers limited means to direct trade or investment. It proposes maintaining commercial ties with China, subject to controls on militarily useful exports.

subfiles.title: Forwarding SCAP letter to Prime Minister Yoshida
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits SCAP’s press release on MacArthur’s stabilization letter.
subfiles.summary: Forwards the December 19 release containing MacArthur’s letter to Yoshida.

subfiles.title: SCAP Letter to Prime Minister on Stabilization
subfiles.about: Presents the U.S. stabilization directive and urges Japanese action.
subfiles.summary: MacArthur links future American assistance to Japanese progress on stabilization and calls for shared austerity and increased production. An appended list gives ten objectives, including budget balance, tax enforcement and a single exchange rate.

subfiles.title: Steering Committee meeting of December 21
subfiles.about: Reports Far Eastern Commission discussion of the stabilization directive and other agenda items.
subfiles.summary: Members debated the urgency and authority for the U.S. directive, Japan’s industrial level, cultural objects, and aircraft and munitions plants.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning Japanese production levels
subfiles.about: Authorizes a response to concerns about production above 1930–34 levels.
subfiles.summary: Explains that Japan’s peaceful-needs policy does not prescribe fixed output for individual industries.

subfiles.title: Cover memorandum for proposed Commission statement
subfiles.about: Transmits a statement for discretionary use.
subfiles.summary: Authorizes use of the enclosed reply to questions raised on January 6.

subfiles.title: Proposed statement on Japanese economic stabilization
subfiles.about: Clarifies the relation between self-support and prewar production levels.
subfiles.summary: Says some industries may exceed 1930–34 output without breaching the Commission’s peaceful-needs policy.

subfiles.title: Army letter on policy for excessive economic concentration
subfiles.about: Requests renewed opposition to a Far Eastern Commission deconcentration proposal.
subfiles.summary: Draper asks State to reaffirm instructions opposing C 2-230/4 and refers to a briefing on Japan’s deconcentration program.

subfiles.title: Instruction to oppose further deconcentration policy
subfiles.about: Directs opposition to C 2-230/4 and similar proposals.
subfiles.summary: Instructs the delegation to prevent adoption of further policy on excessive economic concentration.

subfiles.title: Reply to Draper on deconcentration instructions
subfiles.about: Confirms written instructions opposing C 2-230/4.
subfiles.summary: Saltzman says the delegation already had oral instructions to oppose the proposal and encloses written confirmation. He also notes Hutchinson’s briefing to the Commission committee.

subfiles.title: Enclosed instruction on deconcentration policy
subfiles.about: Repeats instructions to oppose additional deconcentration policy.
subfiles.summary: Directs opposition to C 2-230/4 and any similar proposal.

subfiles.title: Background for luncheon with Secretary Royall
subfiles.about: Prepares discussion points on Japan policy and economic stabilization.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum discusses Dodge’s mission, concern over SCAP’s implementation of stabilization, NSC 13/2, and the Far Eastern Commission’s role. It advises against discussing reparations before State reaches a position.

subfiles.title: Interim Directive to the Supreme Commander: Economic Stabilization in Japan
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Orders a Japanese stabilization program and sets a target for one exchange rate.
subfiles.summary: The directive requires fiscal, monetary, price and wage stability, increased exports, and specific measures on taxes, credit, trade, production and food collection.

subfiles.title: Tokyo economic reporting airgram A-21
subfiles.about: Reports on exchange-rate planning and several Japanese economic developments.
subfiles.summary: Despite heavy OCR damage, the airgram discusses the Dodge mission and exchange-rate questions, then reports on deconcentration, labor disputes and investment arrangements.

subfiles.title: Tokyo economic reporting airgram A-27
subfiles.about: Reports Communist activity around taxes and other commercial matters.
subfiles.summary: The airgram describes Communist involvement in tax protests, American business complaints about occupation authorities, and trade talks with France and Belgium.

subfiles.title: Economic Aid to Japan in Post-Treaty Period
subfiles.about: Urges planning for aid to Japan after a peace treaty.
subfiles.summary: Howard seeks cost and legislative proposals for post-treaty aid to inform treaty, Defense Department and congressional discussions.

subfiles.title: Tokyo airgram on Soviet shipbuilding orders
subfiles.about: Reports a Soviet complaint about Japanese shipbuilding for foreign customers.
subfiles.summary: A Soviet trade representative alleges discrimination after SCAP rejected a vessel order while allowing construction for other countries. The damaged OCR obscures some details.

subfiles.title: Establishment of Free Enterprise System in the Ryukyu Islands
subfiles.about: Reports Ryukyu free enterprise rules and transmits the proclamation and directives.
subfiles.summary: Sebald explains the October 1948 proclamation permitting licensed private trade, easing price and inter-island restrictions, and creating economic committees. He describes rehabilitation funding, a planned Board of Trade, and early signs of increased private commerce.

subfiles.title: Special Proclamation No. 33
subfiles.about: Establishes rules for free enterprise and trade in the Ryukyus.
subfiles.summary: The proclamation defines free enterprise and permits licensed Ryukyuans to trade among island areas and with other residents, subject to restrictions on essential goods. It sets rules for civilian supply imports, currency and import-export administration. The text continues after page 60.
